authored_against: High School Physics, Grade 11. Keys state established science at this course level; they are not extracted from the source, which states a focus and generic objectives.

fixed_facts: Displacement is a vector from start point to end point; distance is the scalar path length travelled.
relationships: Position is stated relative to a chosen origin and reference frame, and the choice must be stated before positions mean anything.
Displacement depends only on start and end points; distance depends on the whole path, so the two differ whenever the path is not straight.
Motion described in one reference frame may be described quite differently in another, and neither description is wrong.
accepted_alternative_framings: Any consistent sign convention and origin are acceptable, provided they are stated and used consistently.
disqualifying_errors: Reporting displacement as equal to distance for a path that is not straight and one-directional.
Describing a position or a motion with no reference frame or origin stated.
Claiming displacement can exceed the distance travelled.
topics.out_of_scope: Relativistic reference frames and non-inertial frame corrections are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Velocity is the rate of change of position; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
Acceleration is non-zero whenever speed changes, direction changes, or both.
relationships: Velocity is a vector: it has magnitude and direction, and speed is its magnitude.
An object moving at constant speed around a curve is accelerating, because its direction, and therefore its velocity, is changing.
Acceleration and velocity are independent in direction: an object can be moving one way and accelerating the other, which is what slowing down is.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming acceleration is always in the direction of motion.
Claiming an object moving at constant speed is never accelerating.
Using speed and velocity interchangeably where direction matters.
topics.out_of_scope: Calculus definitions of instantaneous rate are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: On a position-time graph the slope is velocity; on a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the curve is displacement.
relationships: The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity, including its sign, which carries direction.
The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, and the area between the curve and the time axis gives displacement.
A graph represents the motion; it is not a picture of the path the object took through space.
disqualifying_errors: Reading a position-time graph as a map of the object's path.
Claiming the slope of a velocity-time graph gives velocity, or that its area gives acceleration.
Claiming a horizontal line on a position-time graph shows motion at a constant non-zero speed rather than rest.
topics.out_of_scope: Curve fitting and numerical differentiation of experimental data are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The kinematic relationships for uniform acceleration apply only while the acceleration is constant.
relationships: For constant acceleration, final velocity, displacement, and time are related by the standard kinematic relationships.
Near Earth's surface, an object in free fall with negligible air resistance accelerates downward at approximately nine point eight metres per second squared, independently of its mass.
Applying the relationships requires the acceleration to be constant over the whole interval considered.
accepted_alternative_framings: Any of the standard kinematic equations, or graphical reasoning giving the same result, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Applying the constant-acceleration relationships across an interval where the acceleration changes.
Claiming heavier objects fall with greater acceleration when air resistance is negligible.
Claiming an object at the top of its flight has zero acceleration because its velocity is momentarily zero.
topics.out_of_scope: Air resistance modelling and terminal velocity calculation are beyond this course.

relationships: Every timing and distance measurement carries uncertainty, and that uncertainty propagates into any derived velocity or acceleration.
Repeated trials estimate random uncertainty but do not reveal systematic error such as a mis-set timing gate.
A reported result states its uncertainty, or a reader cannot judge whether two values differ meaningfully.
accepted_alternative_framings: Reporting a range, a mean with spread, or an explicit uncertainty are all acceptable at this level.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming two measured values differ when the difference is smaller than the uncertainty.
Claiming repeated trials remove systematic error.
Reporting a derived quantity to more significant figures than the input measurements support.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal error propagation formulas and statistical hypothesis testing are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Vectors add by components or head-to-tail; they do not add by simple arithmetic unless they are along the same line.
relationships: A vector is fully specified by magnitude and direction and can be resolved into perpendicular components.
Perpendicular components are independent: motion or force in one direction does not affect the other.
The magnitude of a vector sum is generally less than the sum of the magnitudes, and equals it only when the vectors are parallel.
accepted_alternative_framings: Component method and scale diagram method give the same result and are both acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Adding vector magnitudes arithmetically when the vectors are not along the same line.
Claiming horizontal and vertical components of projectile motion affect one another.
Reporting a vector result with magnitude only where direction is required.
topics.out_of_scope: Three-dimensional vector algebra, dot and cross products are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on the chosen object, not the forces that object exerts on others.
relationships: Each force on the diagram has an identified source: another object that is in contact with, or interacting at a distance with, the chosen body.
The two forces of an interaction pair act on different objects and therefore never appear on the same free-body diagram.
Motion itself is not a force, so no arrow is drawn for the object's own movement.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing a force of motion, a force of inertia, or a force the object carries with it.
Including on one diagram both members of an action-reaction pair.
Drawing a force with no identifiable source object.
topics.out_of_scope: Fictitious forces in rotating frames are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Net force is the vector sum of all forces acting on an object, and zero net force means zero acceleration.
relationships: An object with zero net force is either at rest or moving with constant velocity; both are equilibrium states.
Net force determines acceleration, not velocity: a large net force on a slow object is entirely possible.
Forces are summed as vectors, so perpendicular components are treated independently.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an object moving at constant velocity must have a net force acting on it.
Claiming net force determines the direction of motion rather than the direction of acceleration.
Adding force magnitudes arithmetically when the forces are not collinear.
topics.out_of_scope: Torque, rotational equilibrium, and extended-body statics are beyond this course.

topics.focus: Newton's second law as a mathematical relationship
fixed_facts: Acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass, and it is in the direction of the net force.
relationships: For a given mass, doubling the net force doubles the acceleration; for a given net force, doubling the mass halves it.
The relationship applies to the net force, not to any single force acting on the object.
Acceleration is always in the direction of the net force, whatever the direction of motion.
accepted_alternative_framings: Expressing the relationship as an equation, as a proportionality, or in words are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Applying the relationship to one individual force rather than the net force.
Claiming acceleration is in the direction of motion rather than of net force.
Claiming force is proportional to velocity rather than to acceleration.
topics.out_of_scope: Variable-mass systems and the momentum form of the second law are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Mass is a property of the object and does not change with location; weight is the gravitational force on it and does.
relationships: Mass measures how strongly an object resists a change in motion and is measured in kilograms.
Weight is a force, measured in newtons, equal to mass times the local gravitational field strength.
An object in free fall or in orbit still has weight; what it lacks is a supporting normal force, which is why it feels weightless.
disqualifying_errors: Treating mass and weight as the same quantity or reporting one in the other's units.
Claiming an object's mass changes on the Moon.
Claiming orbiting astronauts are weightless because there is no gravity at that altitude.
topics.out_of_scope: Gravitational versus inertial mass equivalence is beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface and is not always equal to the object's weight.
relationships: Friction acts parallel to the contact surface and opposes relative sliding or the tendency to slide.
Frictional force depends on the normal force and on the surfaces, and to a good approximation not on the contact area.
Static friction adjusts up to a maximum to prevent sliding; kinetic friction acts once sliding has begun and is generally smaller.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the normal force always equals the object's weight, including on an incline or when another vertical force acts.
Claiming friction depends principally on contact area.
Claiming friction always opposes motion rather than relative sliding; friction is what propels a walking person forward.
topics.out_of_scope: Rolling resistance, lubrication regimes, and surface physics are beyond this course.

relationships: Force data is interpreted against a stated model, and the model predicts the shape of the relationship as well as its values.
A linear relationship between net force and acceleration supports the second law; departures indicate an unaccounted force such as friction.
The intercept and the scatter of a fitted line carry information about systematic and random error.
disqualifying_errors: Fitting a line through force-acceleration data and ignoring a substantial non-zero intercept.
Attributing a departure from the expected relationship to error without identifying a candidate cause.
Claiming agreement with the model from data whose scatter is too large to distinguish the alternatives.
topics.out_of_scope: Regression statistics and residual analysis are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Momentum is mass times velocity, and it is a vector with the same direction as the velocity.
relationships: Momentum depends on both mass and velocity, so a slow heavy object and a fast light one can carry the same momentum.
Momentum is a vector, so its direction matters and momenta in opposite directions partly cancel.
Momentum and kinetic energy are different quantities and are not interchangeable.
disqualifying_errors: Treating momentum as a scalar and adding magnitudes regardless of direction.
Using momentum and kinetic energy as though they were the same quantity.
Claiming momentum depends on speed alone.
topics.out_of_scope: Relativistic momentum and angular momentum are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: In the absence of a net external force, the total momentum of a system is unchanged by interactions within it.
relationships: Total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after it, provided no net external force acts.
Momentum conservation holds for every collision type, including those where kinetic energy is not conserved.
Defining the system is part of applying the principle: a force is external or internal only with respect to a stated system.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions.
Applying momentum conservation to a system with a substantial unaccounted external force.
Adding momenta as scalars and concluding momentum was not conserved.
topics.out_of_scope: Centre-of-mass frame analysis and two-dimensional collision algebra are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts, and it equals the change in momentum.
relationships: For a given change in momentum, extending the contact time reduces the average force.
This is why crumple zones, airbags, helmets, and catching techniques reduce peak force, without reducing the momentum change.
Impulse is a vector in the direction of the average force.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a protective device reduces the change in momentum rather than the peak force.
Claiming impulse and force are the same quantity.
Claiming a longer contact time increases the force for the same momentum change.
topics.out_of_scope: Force-time curve integration for non-constant forces is acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Momentum is conserved in all collisions; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones.
relationships: In an elastic collision total kinetic energy is unchanged; in an inelastic collision some is transferred to deformation, sound, and thermal energy.
In a perfectly inelastic collision the objects move off together, and kinetic energy loss is at its maximum for that momentum.
Real macroscopic collisions are never perfectly elastic, though some are close enough to model that way.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision.
Claiming momentum is not conserved in an inelastic collision.
Claiming energy is destroyed in an inelastic collision rather than transferred to other forms.
topics.out_of_scope: Coefficient of restitution and elastic collision algebra in two dimensions are beyond this course.

relationships: Analysing a collision requires masses and velocities before and after, with directions, and each carries measurement uncertainty.
A momentum total that does not balance within uncertainty indicates an unaccounted external force or a measurement problem, and both are investigated rather than assumed.
Comparing kinetic energy before and after classifies the collision, and any energy shortfall is accounted for physically.
disqualifying_errors: Concluding momentum was not conserved without checking uncertainty or external forces.
Omitting direction from velocities in a momentum calculation.
Reporting a kinetic energy loss without identifying where the energy went.
topics.out_of_scope: Video tracking analysis methods and statistical treatment of trial sets are beyond this course.

relationships: A protective device works by extending the time or the distance over which momentum changes, thereby reducing peak force.
It can also spread the force over a larger area, reducing pressure, which is a distinct mechanism from reducing the force.
The device is evaluated against measured peak force or deceleration under stated test conditions, not against how sturdy it appears.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a protective device removes the momentum change rather than extending the time over which it occurs.
Confusing spreading force over area with reducing the total force.
Declaring a design effective without a measurement against the stated criterion.
topics.out_of_scope: Materials testing standards and biomechanical injury criteria are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Gravitational attraction between two masses is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
Gravity is always attractive.
relationships: Every pair of masses attracts, with a force that grows with either mass and falls off with the square of separation.
The two objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other regardless of how different their masses are.
The distance in the relationship is between centres, not between surfaces, for spherically symmetric bodies.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming gravity can be repulsive.
Claiming the more massive body exerts the larger gravitational force in a pair.
Using surface separation rather than centre separation for spherical bodies.
topics.out_of_scope: General relativity and gravitational field mapping are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
relationships: Coulomb's law has the same inverse-square form as the gravitational law, but electric charge comes in two signs, so the force can attract or repel.
The two charges exert equal and opposite forces on each other regardless of their relative magnitudes.
The presence of intervening material changes the force, unlike the gravitational case.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the larger charge exerts the greater force in a pair.
Claiming electrostatic force is always attractive.
Claiming the force falls off in direct proportion to distance rather than to its square.
topics.out_of_scope: Dielectric theory, continuous charge distributions, and Gauss's law are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: In an inverse-square relationship, doubling the distance reduces the quantity to one quarter.
relationships: An inverse-square dependence arises whenever an influence spreads outward over a spherical surface whose area grows with the square of the radius.
Doubling the distance quarters the quantity; tripling it reduces the quantity to one ninth.
The relationship never reaches zero at finite distance, so the influence has no sharp boundary.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming doubling the distance halves an inverse-square quantity.
Claiming an inverse-square force becomes exactly zero beyond some distance.
Applying an inverse-square relationship to a quantity that does not spread over a spherical surface without justification.
topics.out_of_scope: Solid angle formalism and flux integration are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The electrostatic force between two charged subatomic particles is enormously stronger than the gravitational force between them.
relationships: Both forces obey an inverse-square law, but the electrostatic force is vastly stronger for elementary particles.
Gravity nonetheless dominates at astronomical scale because bulk matter is very nearly electrically neutral, so positive and negative contributions cancel.
Gravity has no cancellation mechanism, because mass has only one sign.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming gravity is intrinsically the stronger of the two forces.
Claiming electrostatic forces are irrelevant at atomic scale.
Explaining gravity's astronomical dominance by strength rather than by the absence of cancellation.
topics.out_of_scope: The full hierarchy of fundamental forces and coupling constants is beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Field lines are a representation of a field's direction and relative strength; they are not physical objects.
relationships: The direction of a field line at a point gives the direction of the force on a positive test charge, or on a test mass, placed there.
Closer spacing of field lines represents a stronger field.
Field lines never cross, because the field has one direction at each point.
accepted_alternative_framings: Field vector diagrams and field line diagrams convey the same information and are both acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming field lines are physically present in space.
Drawing field lines that cross one another.
Claiming the field exists only along the drawn lines and not between them.
topics.out_of_scope: Field potential surfaces and quantitative field mapping are beyond this course.

relationships: A predicted force follows from the stated relationship, the measured quantities, and their units, and it carries the uncertainty of those measurements.
A prediction states the assumptions it rests on, such as treating a body as a point mass or ignoring intervening material.
The prediction is then compared against measurement, and disagreement is investigated rather than explained away.
disqualifying_errors: Reporting a calculated force with more precision than the inputs support.
Applying a point-mass or point-charge relationship to extended bodies at close range without saying so.
Attributing a disagreement between prediction and measurement to error with no candidate cause identified.
topics.out_of_scope: Numerical modelling of multi-body force systems is beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Kinetic energy depends on mass and on the square of the speed; gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface depends on mass, gravitational field strength, and height above a chosen reference.
relationships: Doubling an object's speed quadruples its kinetic energy, which is why stopping distance grows so steeply with speed.
Potential energy is defined relative to a chosen reference level, and only differences in it are physically meaningful.
Potential energy belongs to a system of interacting objects, such as an object and Earth, not to one object alone.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming kinetic energy is proportional to speed rather than to its square.
Reporting a potential energy without stating the reference level.
Claiming potential energy is stored inside a single object independently of any interaction.
topics.out_of_scope: Elastic potential energy formulas and relativistic kinetic energy are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Energy is conserved: the total energy of a closed system is constant, and energy transfers or transforms rather than being created or destroyed.
relationships: An energy account requires a defined system and boundary, since what counts as a transfer depends on where the boundary lies.
Energy changes form within the system and is transferred across the boundary by work, by heating, or by radiation.
An account that does not balance indicates an unidentified transfer, not a failure of conservation.
accepted_alternative_framings: Energy bar charts, tables, and equations are all acceptable forms for an energy account.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting an energy account in which energy is created or destroyed.
Claiming energy is lost rather than transferred out of the system.
Reporting an energy account with no system boundary stated.
topics.out_of_scope: Mass-energy equivalence in nuclear processes and thermodynamic potentials are beyond this course.

relationships: A computational energy model steps a system forward using stated relationships, and its output depends on the assumptions and inputs supplied.
The model must conserve energy unless a transfer out of the system is explicitly represented.
Model output is a prediction to be compared with measurement, not a substitute for it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Spreadsheet, code, and hand-iterated models are equally acceptable forms.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting model output as though it were measured data.
Building a model in which energy is created or destroyed with no stated transfer.
Reporting model results without stating the assumptions and inputs used.
topics.out_of_scope: Numerical integration error analysis and simulation validation methods are beyond this course.

topics.focus: energy at macroscopic and particle scales
fixed_facts: The thermal energy of an object is the energy associated with the random motion of its particles.
relationships: Macroscopic kinetic energy is associated with the ordered motion of an object as a whole; thermal energy is associated with the random motion of its particles.
Friction and inelastic collisions convert ordered macroscopic energy into random particle energy, which is why they raise temperature.
Energy is conserved across the two scales, so an apparent macroscopic loss appears as a particle-scale gain.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy is destroyed by friction rather than converted to thermal energy.
Claiming a moving object's macroscopic kinetic energy is the same thing as its thermal energy.
Claiming temperature measures the total energy of an object.
topics.out_of_scope: Statistical mechanics and equipartition are beyond this course.

relationships: Energy transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy is dispersed and becomes far harder to use for work.
Dissipation reduces the useful energy available; it does not reduce the total energy.
Every real transfer dissipates some energy, which is why no device is completely efficient.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming dissipated energy has been destroyed.
Claiming a device can transfer all of its input energy to useful output.
Confusing conservation of total energy with conservation of useful energy.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative entropy and exergy analysis are beyond this course.

topics.focus: building and checking an energy budget
relationships: An energy budget lists the energy in the system at the start, the transfers in and out, and the energy at the end, and the two sides must agree within uncertainty.
A shortfall in the budget points to an unaccounted transfer, most often dissipation, and it is identified rather than absorbed into a residual.
Every term in the budget carries the uncertainty of the measurements it came from.
disqualifying_errors: Balancing a budget by inserting an unexplained term.
Claiming a budget balances when the discrepancy exceeds the measurement uncertainty.
Omitting dissipation from a budget for a system with friction or inelastic interaction.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal uncertainty propagation through multi-term budgets is beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles; thermal energy is the total energy of that random motion and also depends on how much material there is.
relationships: Two objects at the same temperature can hold very different amounts of thermal energy, because thermal energy depends on mass and material as well.
Adding thermal energy to a substance raises its temperature, except during a change of state, when it changes particle arrangement instead.
Temperature determines the direction of spontaneous thermal transfer; total thermal energy does not.
disqualifying_errors: Treating temperature and thermal energy as the same quantity.
Claiming the object with more thermal energy is necessarily at the higher temperature.
Claiming temperature rises steadily while a substance is melting or boiling.
topics.out_of_scope: Absolute temperature scales beyond conversion, and kinetic theory derivations, are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Conduction transfers energy through particle interaction, convection through bulk fluid movement, and radiation by electromagnetic waves requiring no medium.
relationships: Conduction requires matter in contact and is fastest in materials with mobile electrons, which is why metals conduct thermally as well as electrically.
Convection requires a fluid free to move, so it does not occur within a solid.
Radiation occurs across a vacuum and is how energy reaches Earth from the Sun.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming convection occurs within a solid.
Claiming thermal radiation requires a medium.
Claiming an insulator produces cold rather than slowing transfer.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative transfer coefficients, Stefan-Boltzmann calculations, and emissivity are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Objects in thermal contact exchange energy until they reach the same temperature; net transfer is then zero.
relationships: Net thermal energy flows from higher to lower temperature, and the flow stops when the temperatures are equal.
At equilibrium, exchange continues in both directions at equal rates, so equilibrium is dynamic rather than static.
Energy is conserved during equilibration: what one body loses, the other and the surroundings gain.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming cold flows from the cooler body to the warmer one.
Claiming all exchange ceases at thermal equilibrium.
Claiming equilibrium means equal thermal energy rather than equal temperature.
topics.out_of_scope: The zeroth law stated formally and quantitative equilibration timescales are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Specific heat capacity is the energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin, and it differs between substances.
relationships: For the same energy input and the same mass, a substance with higher specific heat capacity shows a smaller temperature rise.
Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity, which is why large bodies of water moderate nearby climates.
The energy transferred is the product of mass, specific heat capacity, and temperature change.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming equal energy input produces equal temperature change regardless of substance or mass.
Confusing specific heat capacity with thermal conductivity.
Applying the specific heat relationship across a change of state.
topics.out_of_scope: Latent heat calculations and calorimetry error analysis are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Thermal energy does not flow spontaneously from a cooler body to a warmer one, and no cyclic device converts thermal energy entirely into work.
relationships: Energy spontaneously disperses, so the total disorder of a system and its surroundings does not decrease.
A refrigerator or heat pump moves energy from cooler to warmer only because work is supplied, so the overall dispersal still increases.
This sets an upper limit on the efficiency of any heat engine that is strictly below one hundred per cent.
accepted_alternative_framings: Formulations in terms of entropy, of energy dispersal, or of the impossibility of a perfect engine are equivalent.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a heat engine can be one hundred per cent efficient.
Claiming a local decrease in disorder violates the second law without accounting for the surroundings.
Confusing the first law's conservation of energy with a claim that energy stays equally useful.
topics.out_of_scope: Carnot efficiency calculation and statistical entropy are acceptable but not required.

relationships: Investigating thermal behaviour requires stating the system, its boundary, and the transfers that cross it.
Measured temperature changes are evidence about energy transfer only when mass and material are also known.
Thermal transfer to the environment is present in every real setup, so it belongs in the account rather than being assumed negligible without checking.
disqualifying_errors: Concluding energy was not conserved from an incomplete account of transfers to the surroundings.
Comparing temperature changes for different masses or materials as though they showed equal energy transfers.
Assuming a container is perfectly insulating with no evidence.
topics.out_of_scope: Calorimeter constant determination and formal uncertainty budgets are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Electric fields exert forces on charges whether or not they are moving; magnetic fields exert forces only on moving charges and on magnetic materials.
relationships: A field is a model in which one object modifies the space around it, and a second object responds to the field at its own location.
The electric field direction is defined as the direction of the force on a positive test charge.
Magnetic field lines form closed loops; isolated magnetic poles have never been observed.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a magnetic field exerts a force on a stationary charge.
Claiming isolated magnetic north or south poles can be produced by cutting a magnet.
Treating field lines as physical objects rather than a representation.
topics.out_of_scope: Maxwell's equations, field energy density, and relativistic field transformation are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: An electric current produces a magnetic field around it.
relationships: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field encircling it, and the field strength increases with the current.
Coiling the wire concentrates the field, and adding an iron core strengthens it further, which is how electromagnets work.
A current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field experiences a force, which is the basis of the electric motor.
accepted_alternative_framings: Right-hand rule conventions in any consistent form are acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a stationary charge produces a magnetic field.
Claiming an electromagnet's field persists unchanged when the current is switched off, with no ferromagnetic retention involved.
Claiming the magnetic field of a straight wire points along the wire.
topics.out_of_scope: Ampere's law and quantitative field calculation are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A voltage is induced in a circuit only when the magnetic flux through it is changing.
relationships: Relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field, or a changing field strength, changes the flux and induces a voltage.
A steady magnetic field with no relative motion induces nothing, however strong it is.
The induced effect opposes the change that produced it, which is why generators require work to turn.
accepted_alternative_framings: Faraday's and Lenz's descriptions, whether named or described in plain terms, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a stationary magnet held near a stationary coil induces a steady voltage.
Claiming induction produces energy rather than converting mechanical work into electrical energy.
Claiming the induced effect reinforces the change that produced it.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative flux calculation and transformer design equations are beyond this course.

topics.focus: field models of interaction at a distance
relationships: The field model replaces action at a distance with a local interaction: the source establishes a field, and the field acts on whatever is present at a point.
Changes in a field propagate at finite speed, not instantaneously.
The field model applies to gravitational, electric, and magnetic interactions, with important differences in sign and in what responds.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming field changes propagate instantaneously across any distance.
Claiming a field exists only where a second object is present to feel it.
Treating gravitational and electric fields as identical in behaviour, ignoring that mass has one sign and charge has two.
topics.out_of_scope: Field quantisation and retarded potentials are beyond this course.

relationships: Work is done when a charge or a mass moves through a field along the direction of the force, and energy is transferred as a result.
Moving a charge or mass against the field force increases the system's potential energy; moving with it decreases it.
Energy is conserved throughout: a generator supplies electrical energy only because mechanical work is supplied to it.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a generator or an induction device produces energy.
Claiming potential energy belongs to the moving object alone rather than to the interacting system.
Claiming work is done when motion is perpendicular to the field force.
topics.out_of_scope: Potential difference formalism and field energy density are acceptable but not required.

relationships: An induction investigation varies one factor at a time: relative speed, field strength, number of turns, or orientation.
Detecting no induced effect when nothing is changing is a positive result confirming the model, not a failed trial.
Measurements state the instrument, its sensitivity, and the conditions, since induced voltages are often small.
disqualifying_errors: Reporting an induced voltage under static conditions with no changing flux and attributing it to induction.
Varying several factors at once and attributing the effect to one.
Treating an instrument's limit of detection as evidence that no effect exists.
topics.out_of_scope: Instrumentation design and signal conditioning are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A wave transfers energy without net transport of the medium.
Amplitude is maximum displacement from equilibrium; wavelength is the distance between matching points on successive cycles; frequency is cycles per second; period is the time for one cycle.
relationships: Particles of a medium oscillate about fixed positions while the wave and its energy travel through.
Frequency and period are reciprocals of one another.
In a transverse wave the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of travel; in a longitudinal wave it is along it.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a wave carries the medium along with it.
Confusing amplitude with wavelength, or frequency with wave speed.
Claiming sound is a transverse wave in air.
topics.out_of_scope: Wave equation derivation and polarisation are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.
relationships: In a given medium the wave speed is fixed by the medium, so frequency and wavelength vary inversely with each other.
When a wave crosses into a new medium its frequency is unchanged, set by the source, while its speed and wavelength both change.
The relationship holds for all waves, mechanical and electromagnetic alike.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a wave's frequency changes when it enters a new medium.
Claiming increasing the frequency of a wave in a fixed medium increases its speed.
Claiming wavelength and frequency vary in direct proportion.
topics.out_of_scope: Dispersion relations and group versus phase velocity are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Mechanical waves require a medium; electromagnetic waves do not.
Sound travels faster in solids than in liquids and faster in liquids than in gases.
relationships: The speed of a mechanical wave is set by properties of the medium, principally its stiffness and its density.
Light slows on entering a denser transparent medium and returns to its vacuum speed on leaving.
The wave's frequency is a property of the source and does not change with the medium.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming sound travels faster in air than in water or steel.
Claiming sound can travel through a vacuum.
Claiming light travels faster in glass or water than in vacuum.
topics.out_of_scope: Acoustic impedance and refractive index calculation are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Reflection returns a wave from a boundary, refraction is the change of direction on entering a medium where the speed differs, and diffraction is the spreading of a wave past an edge or through a gap.
relationships: In reflection from a smooth surface the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.
Refraction occurs because the wave speed changes at the boundary; a wave entering along the normal changes speed without changing direction.
Diffraction is most pronounced when the gap or obstacle is comparable in size to the wavelength.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming refraction occurs because the wave's frequency changes at the boundary.
Claiming diffraction is significant regardless of the ratio of wavelength to gap size.
Measuring angles of incidence and reflection from the surface rather than from the normal.
topics.out_of_scope: Snell's law calculation, total internal reflection, and interference are acceptable but not required.

topics.focus: wave and particle models of light
fixed_facts: Light shows wave behaviour such as diffraction and interference, and particle behaviour such as the photoelectric effect; neither model alone accounts for all observations.
relationships: The wave model explains interference, diffraction, and refraction; the particle model explains the photoelectric effect and the discreteness of light emission and absorption.
Which model applies depends on the experiment; the two are not competing claims about which is really true.
Photon energy increases with frequency, which is why the effect of light on matter depends on frequency rather than on brightness alone.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing this as wave-particle duality, or as complementary models each with a domain, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming one of the two models has been shown to be the correct one and the other abandoned.
Claiming photon energy depends on the brightness of the light rather than on its frequency.
Claiming light requires a medium to travel through.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantum mechanics, the photoelectric equation, and de Broglie wavelength are acceptable to reference but not required.

relationships: Competing models are evaluated on the range of observations each accounts for and on the predictions that distinguish them.
A decisive test is one where the models predict different outcomes, so an observation consistent with both settles nothing.
A model retained for a limited domain is not thereby wrong; its domain is part of the model.
disqualifying_errors: Selecting between models on evidence consistent with both.
Claiming a model with a limited domain has been refuted.
Choosing a model on simplicity or familiarity alone with no evidential comparison.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal model selection criteria and philosophy of science are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: In order of increasing frequency and decreasing wavelength the spectrum runs radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in vacuum, approximately three times ten to the eighth metres per second.
relationships: The regions of the spectrum differ in frequency and wavelength, not in their fundamental nature.
Photon energy increases with frequency, so gamma rays carry far more energy per photon than radio waves.
Only the higher-frequency regions, from roughly ultraviolet upward, carry enough energy per photon to ionise atoms.
accepted_alternative_framings: Ordering the spectrum by wavelength or by frequency are equally correct, provided the direction is stated.
disqualifying_errors: Placing the spectrum regions out of order, such as putting ultraviolet below visible in frequency.
Claiming different regions of the spectrum travel at different speeds in vacuum.
Claiming radio waves or microwaves are ionising radiation.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative photon energy calculation is acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Whether radiation is absorbed, transmitted, or reflected depends on both the material and the frequency of the radiation.
relationships: Absorption transfers energy from the radiation to the material, commonly raising its temperature or exciting its electrons.
A material transparent to one part of the spectrum can be opaque to another, which is why glass passes visible light but blocks much ultraviolet.
Ionising radiation damages matter by removing electrons from atoms, which non-ionising radiation cannot do however intense it is.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a material behaves the same way toward all frequencies of radiation.
Claiming non-ionising radiation causes ionisation if it is intense enough.
Claiming absorbed radiation energy disappears rather than being transferred to the material.
topics.out_of_scope: Attenuation coefficients, dosimetry, and spectroscopy are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Digital signals encode information in discrete values; analog signals vary continuously.
relationships: Noise added to an analog signal becomes part of it, while a digital signal can be restored by rounding each value to the nearest allowed level.
That restorability is why digital signals survive repeated transmission and copying far better than analog ones.
Digitising a continuous signal involves sampling and rounding, so it loses some information; how much depends on the sampling and the levels used.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming digital signals are unaffected by noise or loss.
Claiming digitisation preserves the original signal exactly.
Claiming an analog signal can be cleaned of accumulated noise as a digital one can.
topics.out_of_scope: Sampling theorem, quantisation error analysis, and coding theory are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The distinction between ionising and non-ionising radiation is set by photon energy, which depends on frequency, not by the power of the source.
relationships: Evaluating a claim about radiation means identifying which part of the spectrum is involved, at what intensity, and over what exposure.
A claim's strength depends on the study design and on whether independent work agrees, not on the confidence of the presentation.
The word radiation covers everything from radio waves to gamma rays, so a claim about radiation that does not specify which is not evaluable.
disqualifying_errors: Treating all radiation as equivalent in its effects on matter or on people.
Claiming a non-ionising source becomes ionising at high power.
Accepting or rejecting a published claim without reference to the evidence or the study design behind it.
topics.out_of_scope: Epidemiological methods, exposure standards, and health physics are beyond this course.

relationships: Wave-based technologies work by encoding information onto a wave, transmitting it, and decoding it, and each stage constrains performance.
The choice of frequency band is set by how the wave interacts with the environment: penetration, range, and available bandwidth all depend on it.
Every link has limits on range, rate, and reliability set by physics as well as by equipment.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a communication technology has no physical limit on range or data rate.
Claiming frequency band choice is arbitrary rather than driven by propagation behaviour.
Claiming information travels without any physical carrier.
topics.out_of_scope: Modulation schemes, antenna theory, and link budget calculation are beyond this course.

relationships: An energy conversion device is evaluated on measured input, measured useful output, and the difference between them.
No device converts all input to useful output, so an efficiency claim of one hundred per cent indicates a measurement or accounting error.
Design improvements are tested one change at a time against the stated criteria.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a device produces more energy than it receives.
Reporting an efficiency without stating what was measured as input and as useful output.
Changing several design features at once and attributing the improvement to one.
topics.out_of_scope: Thermodynamic efficiency limits for specific cycles and formal design optimisation are beyond this course.
